paper.title: MD-HIT: Machine learning for material property prediction with dataset redundancy control
paper.research_summary: This paper addresses the problem of overestimated machine learning model performance in materials science due to dataset redundancy—i.e., highly similar materials in training and test sets causing information leakage. It proposes MD-HIT, a redundancy reduction algorithm inspired by bioinformatics' CD-HIT, with two variants: MD-HIT-composition (using composition-based distance metrics like Mendeleev and MatScholar) and MD-HIT-structure (using structure-based metrics like XRD and OFM features). The authors apply MD-HIT to Materials Project datasets for formation energy and band gap prediction, demonstrating that redundancy-controlled splits yield lower but more realistic and generalizable (especially out-of-distribution) ML performance compared to standard random splits.

tasks.task_name_raw: dataset redundancy control for material property prediction
tasks.objective: Reduce sample redundancy in material datasets to enable objective, realistic evaluation of ML models’ true predictive capability—particularly extrapolation and out-of-distribution performance—by preventing information leakage between training and test sets.
constraints: avoid overestimation of ML model performance
enable fair comparison across models and properties
support both composition-based and structure-based inputs
input_requirements: distance metrics (e.g., Mendeleev, MatScholar, XRD, OFM)
output_goal: datasets where no pair of samples exceeds a user-defined similarity threshold

evidence.text: In this paper, we survey the overestimated ML performance in materials science for material property prediction and propose MD-HIT, a redundancy reduction algorithm for material datasets.
We propose and develop two material dataset redundancy-reducing algorithms based on a greedy algorithm inspired by the peer bioinformatics CD-HIT algorithm.

stages.stage_goal: Generate non-redundant composition datasets by iteratively selecting representative materials based on composition similarity thresholds.

evidence.text: Our MD-HIT-composition and MD-HIT-structure redundancy reduction algorithms are designed based on this idea, utilizing greedy incremental algorithms. In our case, MD-HIT starts the selection process with a seed material (default to H2O) and then sorts the remaining materials by the number of atoms instead of the formula lengths. Subsequently, it classifies each material as redundant or representative, depending on its similarity to the existing representatives already selected into the cluster.

stages.stage_goal: Generate non-redundant structure datasets by iteratively selecting representative crystal structures based on structure similarity thresholds.

evidence.text: MD-HIT-structure algorithm uses the same greedy adding approach as the MD-HIT-composition, except that it uses a structure-based distance metric.

MD-HIT-structure algorithm also starts the selection process with a seed material (default to H2O) which is put in the non-redundant set. It then sorts the remaining materials in the candidate set by the number of atoms instead of the formula lengths, and classifies them one-by-one as redundant or representative materials based on their similarities (we use Euclidean distance of XRD features or OFM features) to the existing representatives already selected into the non-redundant set.

stages.stage_name_raw: download and curate Materials Project datasets
stages.stage_goal: Acquire raw material data from Materials Project and perform initial filtering to ensure compatibility with downstream redundancy control.

evidence.text: We downloaded 125,619 cif files with material structures from the Materials Project database, which includes 89,354 materials with unique compositions. In cases where compositions corresponded to multiple polymorphs, we adopted average material property values by default, with the exception of formation energy property, for which we used the minimum value. Additionally, we excluded mp-101974 (HeSiO2) due to issues with calculating Matscholar features. After eliminating formulas with over 50 atoms, we obtained a non-duplicate composition dataset with 86,741 samples...

stages.stage_goal: Assess how redundancy control affects prediction accuracy (MAE, R²) of ML models on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution test sets.
stage_output: R² and MAE scores for formation energy and band gap prediction

evidence.text: To investigate the impact of redundancy control on the performance of ML models for predicting material properties, we conducted experiments using datasets filtered by Mendeleev and Matscholar distances.
evidence.section: Composition based material property prediction with redundancy control

evidence.section: Structure based material property prediction with redundancy control

stages.stage_goal: Demonstrate that models trained on non-redundant data achieve better out-of-distribution prediction performance than those trained on redundant data.
stage_output: MAE and R² improvements on OOD test set (10.03% MAE, 31.6% R² gain)

evidence.text: We found that the Roostnr significantly outperforms Roostred model, with 10.03% improvement in MAE and a 31.6% improvement in R2 for the OOD test set. This result demonstrates that removing redundant data can steer an ML model away from focusing on crowded samples, ensuring equitable attention to all other samples, and consequently improving OOD prediction performance.
We downloaded 125,619 cif files with material structures from the Materials Project database, which includes 89,354 materials with unique compositions.

Materials databases such as Materials Project and OpenQuantumMaterials Database (OQMD)11,12 are characterized by the existence of many redundant (highly similar) materials due to the tinkering approach historically used in material design13–15.
For Mendeleev similarity, we used distance thresholds of 0.5, 0.8, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, and 3 to generate seven non-redundant datasets (Mendeleev-nr). The dataset sizes range from 86,740 to 3177.
Similarly, we generated eight Matscholar non-redundant datasets (Matscholar-nr) with percentages of the total range from 50.82% to 2.33%.
We also applied the MD-HIT-structure algorithm to all 125,619 structures and used different thresholds to generate seven XRD non-redundant datasets and eight OFM non-redundant datasets.
We also applied the MD-HIT-structure algorithm to all 125,619 structures and used different thresholds to generate seven XRD non-redundant datasets and eight OFM non-redundant datasets.

To compare the true OOD performance of models trained on non-redundant and redundant dataset, we prepared another OOD test set named EmbeddingOOD. First, we used a pretrained Roost model as an encoder to obtain the latent representations for all samples in the entire dataset (86,740 samples). We then calculated the pairwise distances of all samples using their latent representations and selected 1000 OOD samples that are furthest away on average from their three nearest neighbors, forming our EmbeddingOOD test set.
